segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: His work focuses on next generation nuclear technologies and their role in sustainable energy solutions. segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Fantastic. Thank you very much. Thank you, Christian, for your kind introduction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And thank you to the hosts for the fantastic event so far. Very honored to be here. I'm here to present our reactor design that we've been working on for a few years now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can you see anything? Even icons. Hello?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can you hear me? Poor choice of colors. Yeah, so what are we trying to do?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And why are we here? The goal of the design is to serve communities that are off grid, where the grid is either too expensive or just geographically impossible to connect your electricity generation with your customers. This sector is currently served by diesel generators, which have very complicated and costly logistics of fuel supply, and obviously emit CO2 and other gases.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So we're trying to displace that by offering reactor design that serves the needs of those communities who are focusing on mining, but also on bringing development to those remote communities that will benefit greatly from small nuclear generation. So we converge on five megawatt electric design, which provides either electricity exclusively or a mix of high temperature heat, which is delivered at 500 degrees C. So that's temperature range is inaccessible to light water reactor technologies, but is low enough not to require exotic materials to construct the reactor.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It's 30 years lifetime, sort of compatible with what a mining industry would want. And it runs on a 10 year refueling cycle. The numbers for cost of electricity may strike you as prohibitively high, but I can tell you right now, micro nuclear reactors will never be able to compete with large energy generation on the grid.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: But it's extremely competitive with those off-grid situations where most of the minerals are now existent but inaccessible because of the cost of energy. So that makes accessibility of those minerals possible. One of our briefs for the technology design is to have absolute minimal on-site construction.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So we're aiming at fast deployment times and using conventional transportation, both legal frameworks and things like dimensions and weights that are legally possible today. We're not hoping for any kind of any kind of future legislation that may or may not come up to enable our design. And we promise to take everything back, so returning the sites to brownfield state.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: OK, so what makes it competitive? So it's a combination of design choices. Both fuel and coolant are unique.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There is no other technology that uses that same combination, although they have all been used in other industries or in other reactor designs. So they have a proven track record of both manufacturing supply chain, compatibility of materials with each other, and so forth. So first, low pressure coolant.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So we're using molten salt, which has been used in concentrated solar power plants for many decades. It's been pumped around. And the infrastructure and supply chain for components, pipes, and valves, and flanges, and pumps, they all exist off the shelf with proven track record of availability and performance.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: One of the key features, as I said, is high temperature, but not too high, and low pressure. So we don't need a pressure vessel. We just need a vessel that holds all the components together.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The size of the reactor also enables or offers opportunities for mass manufacturing, which is where the economic case for small reactors or microreactors lies in. So things like hot isostatic pressing, HIP, which is limited by the size of the component. So fewer welds, more mass-produced throughput of production in factories is enabled, actually, by this small size.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We secured partnerships with key component suppliers, both on power conversion side and the reactor side. We're using fuel that is commonly used in research reactors, known as TRIGA, and has a long track record of being used in research reactors. It's incredibly safe, and it's very compact, because moderator hydrogen sits inside fuel pins and makes it very safe, which I'll also talk about in the next slide.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We are very flexible in terms of fuel supply chain. So many microreactors, if not all of them, rely on so-called HALU, 20% enriched uranium, for which the supply chain at the moment doesn't exist. Many countries are trying to gear up for that, but we're not vulnerable to this.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: We very straightforwardly can trade fuel cycle length or refueling cycle for enrichment. We also don't use arguably very expensive and yet to be proven in terms of manufacturing trisulfur, so microparticle fuel, that that supply chain doesn't exist either. So we're free of those.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And so all these things provide regulatory certainty that has been highlighted previously, that is sort of an important enabling factor. And maybe the last but not least thing to mention is being affiliated with the University of Cambridge and teaching nuclear engineering for many years, we also take custody of the human supply chain. So reactors don't exist in a vacuum.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Having hardware is not enough. You need people who understand the technology on both sides, both the regulatory side and the operator side. So we're offering that as well.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Can we do the click again? Next slide. Okay, so this is my last slide, that last bit of the homework.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Why do we think this is safe and secure? As I mentioned, research reactors have been running on uranium zirconium hydride fuel for many years. And it's famous for being very tolerant to reactive perturbations.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Many of those exist on the university campuses and a fast withdrawal of all control rods creating multi-gigawatt pulses is something that these reactors do every day for students' entertainment. So in the context of a power reactor, it provides a very reliable natural feedback mechanism for shutdown. Low pressure coolant, there is nothing that tries to break through.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: As I already mentioned, it's also non-toxic and non-reactive. It also has a good ability to retain fission products in case of fuel failures. This is the salt that is used for curing bacon, basically.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So it is, before radiation, you can lick it. Small size, so quarter of a football pitch is good to make it sort of unattractive as a terrorist target. Low enriched uranium also helps to calm down nerves of the international community in terms of nuclear proliferation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And there's passive decay heat removal that in all situations, you can walk away and the reactor will shut itself down and cool itself. It's not straightforward, but it can be done. And the smaller the reactor, the easier this task becomes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So this becomes an advantage and leads to a pretty straightforward safety case. We are site agnostic. We don't require any water on site, again, for the purpose of having this technology deployed in a wide range of situations.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So everything is air-cooled. So the power conversion cycle rejects heat to air and also a decay heat in case of emergencies is rejected passively to air. I'll finish here and welcome everyone to stop by our booth where we can have more detailed conversation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I appreciate these few minutes are not enough and I had a few technical terms. So thank you very much. Thank you very much for the nice presentation.

segments.text: The core damage frequency, CDF, must be less than 10 to nine for first reactor year. To meet this strategy target, the ISML adapt to fully passive safety system with a fail-safe design and no dependence on external electric power. Next, the economic goal.

segments.text: The construction cost for four modules is targeted at $35,000 US dollar per kilowatt electric and the levelized cost of electric city, LCOE, is targeted at $65 per megawatt hour. segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Looking back through history, every industrial revolution is essentially an energy revolution. Today, we are in the AI revolution era. For Africa to seize this opportunity to achieve economic development, it must build a more stable, continuous and reliable power foundation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Let me look at China's situation. Last year, China's total electricity generation exceeded 10,000 terawatt hours, the largest in the world. Today, China's power demand is no longer driven by traditional industry, but by technology.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It means the power system must evolve towards flexibility and resilience. And that is precisely the design philosophy of SMRs. To ensure energy security, China's nuclear power has grown steady and now leads the world.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The total scale, including the operation and approved units, has reached 112 reactors, also the largest in the world. And the CNC is the leading force of China's nuclear power development. Our SMR technology, ACP-100 and HTR-PM is in commercial deployment.

segments.text: And as China's sole reactor exporter, we have successfully delivered seven power reactors overseas through our integrated financing EPC and OM service. segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I want to emphasize here that China's SMR has already been commercially deployed, ahead of many other SMR technologies around the world. And specifically, the ACP-100 right now is under commissioning stage, and the commercial operation is expected this year. And the HTGR has already been in commercial operation since 2023.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: This marks China's successful transition of SMRs from engineering demonstration to scalable commercial deployment. So for the situation in Africa, the African continent now is undergoing a profound transformation of industrialization and urbanization. Yet its power system still faces a series of challenges, including the fragile grid transmission bottlenecks and also the physical constraints.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The flexible characteristics of SMR happen to highly match Africa's current development stage. And based on this understanding, we have tailored the 60 engine solution for Africa using the world's most mature and proven Chinese SMR technology. And the first key is technological maturity.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: China's SMR is not a concept in the lab, but an engineering system already in commercial operation. The value for Africa is very obvious. It will eliminate the technology uncertainty, providing reliable and safe best load of power.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The second key is transformable deployment. It will benefit a small grid and isolated industrial systems with excellent grid adaptability and deployment flexibility. And for the third key is the trusted bankability.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Through faster deployment and standardized modular construction, we significantly reduce the one-time capital investment and make nuclear energy economically investable. The fourth key is the trinket delivery. CNC's one-stop integrated solution covers EPC operation support and the fuel supply, ensuring the long-term safe operation of nuclear power plants.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And the fifth key is transformational partnership. SMR can help African countries leap from power projects to integrated industrial development. It will drive the economy from raw material exporter to industrial producer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: And the last key is transparency and regulatory support. Based on our SMR experience, we can enable transparent and trusted nuclear power deployment and help to build a robust regulation framework. In summary, SMR is a transformational energy engine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It will provide Africa with a dispatchable best load of power and support a long-term energy security. Therefore, SMR is far more than a power plant. It's a platform for Africa's future development.
